title: Φιλάργυρος
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 344 (= Perry 225). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Φιλάργυρός τις, ἅπασαν αὐτοῦ τὴν οὐσίαν ἐξαργυρισάμενος καὶ χρυσοῦν βῶλον ποιήσας, ἔν τινι τόπῳ κατώρυξε συγκατορύξας ἐκεῖ καὶ τὴν ψυχὴν ἑαυτοῦ καὶ τὸν νοῦν, καὶ καθ’ ἡμέραν ἐρχόμενος αὐτὸν ἔβλεπε.
sentences.tr: Philargyros tis, hapasan autou tēn ousian exargyrisamenos kai chrysoun bōlon poiēsas, en tini topōi katōryxe synkatoryxas ekei kai tēn psychēn heautou kai ton noun, kai kath’ hēmeran erchomenos auton eblepe.
sentences.l: A certain miser, having turned all his property into cash and made a lump of gold, buried it in a certain place, burying there along with it his own soul and his mind as well, and coming each day he would look at it.
sentences.i: A miser turned everything he had into money, made it into a lump of gold, and buried it in a certain place — burying his soul and his wits there along with it — and came every day to look at it.
sentences.n: φιλάργυρος is the silver-lover, and ἐξαργυρίζομαι, 'turn into silver', is the ordinary word for realising an estate in cash. συγκατορύσσω keeps the κατορύσσω of the main verb and adds συν-: what he buried with the gold was himself.

sentences.t: Τῶν δὲ ἐργατῶν τις αὐτὸν παρατηρήσας καὶ τὸ γεγονὸς συννοήσας, ἀνορύξας τὸν βῶλον ἀνείλετο.
sentences.tr: Tōn de ergatōn tis auton paratērēsas kai to gegonos synnoēsas, anoryxas ton bōlon aneileto.
sentences.l: And one of the workmen, having kept watch on him and having understood what had happened, having dug up the lump, took it for himself.
sentences.i: One of the workmen kept watch on him, understood what was going on, dug up the lump and took it for himself.
sentences.n: Three aorist participles hung on a single finite verb — the engine of these fables, where English wants a string of main verbs. τὸ γεγονός is 'the thing that had come about'; ἀνείλετο is middle, taking it up for himself.

sentences.t: Μετὰ δὲ ταῦτα κἀκεῖνος ἐλθὼν καὶ κενὸν τὸν τόπον ἰδὼν θρηνεῖν ἤρξατο καὶ τίλλειν τὰς τρίχας.
sentences.tr: Meta de tauta kakeinos elthōn kai kenon ton topon idōn thrēnein ērxato kai tillein tas trichas.
sentences.l: And after this he too, having come and having seen the place empty, began to wail and to tear his hair.
sentences.n: κενόν stands predicatively: he saw the place to be empty, not 'saw the empty place'.

sentences.t: Τοῦτον δέ τις ὀλοφυρόμενον οὕτως ἰδὼν καὶ τὴν αἰτίαν πυθόμενος· « Μὴ οὕτως, εἶπεν, ὦ οὗτος, ἀθύμει· οὐδὲ γὰρ ἔχων τὸν χρυσὸν εἶχες.
sentences.tr: Touton de tis olophyromenon houtōs idōn kai tēn aitian pythomenos· « Mē houtōs, eipen, ō houtos, athymei· oude gar echōn ton chryson eiches.
sentences.l: And someone, having seen him lamenting so and having inquired the cause: « Do not be downcast so, he said, you there; for you did not have the gold even when you had it.
sentences.i: And someone saw him wailing like this and asked the reason: « Do not take it so hard, my man, he said; for you did not have the gold even when you had it.
sentences.n: The sentence has no main verb outside the speech: εἶπεν is tucked into the quotation as a parenthesis, and the two participles wait for it there. ἔχων … εἶχες grants the having with the participle and denies it with the finite verb.

sentences.t: Λίθον οὖν ἀντὶ χρυσοῦ λαβὼν θὲς καὶ νόμιζέ σοι τὸν χρυσὸν εἶναι· τὴν αὐτὴν γάρ σοι πληρώσει χρείαν· ὡς ὁρῶ γάρ, οὐδ’, ὅτε ὁ χρυσὸς ἦν, ἐν χρήσει ἦσθα τοῦ κτήματος. »
sentences.tr: Lithon oun anti chrysou labōn thes kai nomize soi ton chryson einai· tēn autēn gar soi plērōsei chreian· hōs horō gar, oud’, hote ho chrysos ēn, en chrēsei ēstha tou ktēmatos. »
sentences.l: So take a stone and lay it there in place of the gold, and think the gold is yours; for it will fill the same need for you; for as I see, not even when the gold was there were you in the use of the property. »
sentences.i: So take a stone and put it there instead of the gold, and count the gold as yours; it will serve you the same turn — for as far as I can see, not even while the gold was there were you making any use of it. »
sentences.n: σοι … εἶναι is the dative of possession: 'that the gold is yours'. ἐν χρήσει εἶναι with the genitive is 'to be in the use of' a thing. The whole speech turns on χρῆσις against κτῆσις, use against ownership, which the moral then names outright.

sentences.t: Ὁ μῦθος δηλοῖ ὅτι οὐδὲν ἡ κτῆσις, ἐὰν μὴ ἡ χρῆσις προσῇ.
sentences.tr: Ho mythos dēloi hoti ouden hē ktēsis, ean mē hē chrēsis prosēi.
sentences.l: The fable shows that possession is nothing, if use is not there besides.
sentences.n: No copula is written with οὐδέν — 'possession, nothing' — as regularly in maxims of this shape. πρόσειμι is 'be there in addition'; κτῆσις and χρῆσις chime in the Greek, and the chime is half the point.
